args.line: Authentication-Results: mx.example.com; spf=pass smtp.mailfrom=example.com; dkim=pass header.d=example.com; dmarc=pass header.from=example.com

signals.label: Sender Authentication Passed
signals.detail: SPF, DKIM and DMARC all passed, so the message genuinely came from the domain it claims. That confirms the sender, not their intent — a compromised account passes every one of these.

signals.label: DMARC Failure
signals.detail: The message failed DMARC. It is not authorized by the domain it claims to come from — the strongest single indicator of sender spoofing available from headers alone.

signals.label: SPF Failure
signals.detail: The sending server is not on the list of servers authorized to send for this domain.

signals.label: DKIM Failure
signals.detail: The cryptographic signature did not validate. The message content or its headers were altered after signing, or the signature was forged outright.

cases.name: SPF softfail, DKIM none, DMARC none

signals.label: No DMARC Policy
signals.detail: The sending domain publishes no DMARC policy, so nothing prevents another server from spoofing it and nothing here can confirm the sender either way.

signals.label: SPF Softfail
signals.detail: SPF returned a soft failure or neutral result, so the sending server is only weakly authorized for this domain.

signals.label: No DKIM Signature
signals.detail: The message was not signed with DKIM, so there is no cryptographic evidence tying it to the sending domain.

signals.label: No Authentication Results
signals.detail: This message carries no Authentication-Results header, so SPF/DKIM/DMARC couldn't be checked at all. Common for mail that bypassed normal filtering, and it means the checks below are working with less to go on.

cases.name: Reply-To on a different domain than From

signals.label: Replies Go to a Different Domain
signals.detail: Hitting reply sends your response to "freemail.example", not "company.example". This is how a conversation gets quietly redirected to the attacker, and it is the standard setup for business email compromise.

cases.name: forged trailing Authentication-Results (spf/dkim/dmarc=pass) beyond the Received count is discarded; the real receiving server's fail wins

args.line: Received: from mx.example.com (mx.example.com [198.51.100.1]) by inbound.example.com with ESMTP; Mon, 1 Jan 2024 10:00:00 +0000

signals.label: Authentication-Results Header Predates Real Delivery
signals.detail: The message carries more Authentication-Results headers than it has Received headers to have stamped them — meaning at least one could not have been added by a real mail server relaying the message, and was instead already present in the content as sent. A real server only ever adds this header at the moment it performs the check, never earlier. The extra header was ignored when determining SPF/DKIM/DMARC status below.
